protocol_source: NVBDCP Drug Policy 2013 (rev 2019), Section 3.1
notes: First-line for PV malaria. Resistance reported in Papua — monitor. Give with food to reduce GI side effects.

protocol_source: NVBDCP Drug Policy 2013 (rev 2019), Section 3.1
notes: MANDATORY for PV radical cure (hypnozoite clearance). CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency and pregnancy — screen first. Skip in 1st trimester. Higher dose (0.5mg/kg) in Oceania strains.

protocol_source: NVBDCP Drug Policy 2013 (rev 2019), Section 3.2
notes: First-line for PF malaria per NVBDCP. Available as AS25+AQ67.5 (child <15kg), AS50+AQ135 (15-35kg), AS100+AQ270 (>35kg). DO NOT use as monotherapy — must be given as fixed-dose combination.

protocol_source: NVBDCP Drug Policy 2013 (rev 2019), Section 3.2
notes: Single dose for PF gametocyte clearance (reduces transmission). NOT for radical cure. Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, pregnancy.

protocol_source: NVBDCP Drug Policy 2013, Section 4 (Severe Malaria)
notes: WHO recommends over IV Quinine as first-line for severe malaria. Switch to oral ACT as soon as patient can tolerate. Adjunct: Dextrose infusion (hypoglycaemia common).

protocol_source: NVBDCP Drug Policy 2013, Section 4 (alternate if artesunate unavailable)
notes: Use only if IV Artesunate unavailable. Risk of hypoglycaemia and cinchonism. Must be diluted in Normal Saline/Dextrose for IV.

protocol_source: DGHS Dengue Clinical Management Guidelines 2021, Section 5
notes: ONLY safe antipyretic in dengue. NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) and aspirin STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED — risk of dengue haemorrhagic complications. Do NOT exceed 4g/day (hepatotoxicity risk).

protocol_source: DGHS Dengue Guidelines 2021; WHO Dengue Guidelines 2012
notes: All dengue patients should be encouraged to drink at least 5 glasses of fluids per day (water, ORS, fruit juice, coconut water). ORS is first-line for outpatient dengue with warning signs.

protocol_source: DGHS Dengue Guidelines 2021, Sections 7-8 (DHF/DSS management)
notes: Only for Grade II-IV dengue (DHF/DSS) requiring hospitalisation. Approximately 15-30% of dengue cases progress to DHF. Monitor haematocrit closely — over-hydration risk.

protocol_source: IDSP Cholera Management Protocol; WHO Technical Report 2017
notes: ORS is the primary treatment for 80% of cholera cases. Severe dehydration requires IV Ringer's Lactate (not included separately). WHO cholera protocol: 75mL/kg in first 4 hours.

protocol_source: IDSP Cholera Protocol; WHO Cholera Factsheet 2023
notes: Adjunct to ORS — reduces duration and severity. Doxycycline CONTRAINDICATED in children <8 years and pregnancy — use Erythromycin or Azithromycin instead. Resistance monitoring required; local antibiogram should guide choice.

protocol_source: IMNCI India Adaptation 2017; National ORS Programme MoHFW
notes: Universal first-line treatment for all acute diarrhoea. Low-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L) recommended by WHO since 2004 — reduces need for IV therapy by 33% in children.

drug_class: Micronutrient — reduces diarrhoea duration and severity
protocol_source: IMNCI India 2017; WHO/UNICEF Joint Statement on Zinc 2004
notes: MANDATORY per IMNCI for all children under 5 with diarrhoea. Reduces duration by 25%, severity by 30%. <6 months: 10mg/day; ≥6 months: 20mg/day. NOT indicated for adults in IMNCI protocol.

protocol_source: RNTCP/NTP India Technical Guidelines 2016; revised 2020
notes: Weight bands: <30kg=2 tabs, 30-54kg=3 tabs, 55-69kg=4 tabs, ≥70kg=5 tabs. DOTS strategy — directly observed therapy required. Monitor LFT monthly; Ethambutol — check visual acuity monthly. Rifampicin turns urine/secretions orange — warn patients.

protocol_source: RNTCP/NTP India Technical Guidelines 2016; revised 2020
notes: Continuation phase follows 2-month intensive phase. Total course for new patient: 6 months. For retreatment (Cat II): 2HRZES/1HRZE/5HRE — different FDC kits.

protocol_source: NPCDCS Standard Treatment Protocol 2016; JNC 8 Guidelines
notes: CHRONIC medication — demand modelled per PREVALENT PATIENT, not case. First-line for HTN in India (JNC 8; ESC 2018). Well-tolerated; ankle oedema is common side effect. Pregnancy: safe in 2nd/3rd trimester (Cat C).

protocol_source: NPCDCS Standard Treatment Protocol 2016
notes: CHRONIC — 30-day supply per patient. Preferred in diabetic nephropathy. CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogenic, Cat D). Check serum K+ — risk of hyperkalaemia.

protocol_source: NPCDCS Standard Treatment Protocol 2016
notes: CHRONIC — add-on therapy when monotherapy insufficient. Used in ~40% of hypertension patients (as combination therapy). Monitor electrolytes — risk of hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.

protocol_source: NPCDCS Standard Treatment Protocol 2016; ADA Standards 2024
notes: CHRONIC — 30-day supply. First-line for ALL T2DM without contraindications. Reduces CV mortality (UKPDS). CONTRAINDICATED: eGFR <30, liver disease, contrast dye procedures. GI side effects — take with food. Start at 500mg OD, titrate up.

protocol_source: NPCDCS Standard Treatment Protocol 2016; India EDL 2022
notes: CHRONIC. Second-line or combination with Metformin. HIGH hypoglycaemia risk — educate patients. Avoid in elderly (long half-life, prolonged hypoglycaemia risk). Contraindicated in renal impairment.

protocol_source: NPCDCS 2016; India EDL 2022; ADA 2024
notes: CHRONIC. Required by ~20-25% of T2DM patients (ICMR INDIAB survey). Cold chain storage mandatory (2-8°C). Requires insulin syringes (separately stocked). Dose titrated by fasting blood glucose — not fixed.

drug_class: Iron supplement + haematinic — first-line anaemia treatment
protocol_source: National Iron+ Initiative MoHFW 2013; NFHS-5 treatment arm
notes: Standard IFA RED tablet (60mg Fe + 0.5mg FA) for treatment. IFA BLUE (100mg Fe + 0.5mg FA) for pregnant women. Take with Vitamin C (lemon juice) — improves absorption. Avoid with milk, tea, coffee — reduce absorption by 40-70%. Prevention dose (WIFS): 1 tablet/week for adolescent girls.

drug_class: IV iron complex — severe or non-responsive iron deficiency
protocol_source: India EDL 2022; ICMR Guidelines for IDA 2020
notes: For Hb <7g/dL unresponsive to oral iron, or pre-surgery. Faster repletion than oral iron (days vs weeks). Administer over 15 min IV infusion — observe for anaphylaxis. Approximately 10-15% of diagnosed anaemia cases require IV iron.
